title: Stories into equations, and the traverse
summary: Turn shop stories into equations and solve them end to end, plot the profit line and read what one more unit is worth, then sit eight mixed peaks in one go with no clock and finish the month's monster.

problems.prompt: Speed round: what is 39 times 41?
explanation: 39 and 41 sit the same distance, 1, on either side of the round number 40.
That makes it a difference of squares: 40 squared minus 1 squared, which is 1600 minus 1.
1600 minus 1 is 1599.
problems.useAgain: when two numbers sit the same distance above and below a round number, since their product is always the round number squared minus that distance squared.
hints: Check how far 39 and 41 each sit from the same round number.
Once you have that round number and that distance, square each of them instead of multiplying 39 by 41 directly.
problems.socraticHint: Why does it matter that 39 and 41 are the same distance from 40, rather than two unrelated numbers?

variant.prompt: Speed round: what is 48 times 52?

problems.prompt: In your head. Suppose the fixed costs of a run were 18 dollars, and every unit sold leaves 3 dollars once its own materials are paid for. How many units sold gets you back to zero?
explanation: The 18 dollars is a hole, and each unit sold fills 3 dollars of it.
Count up in threes: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18. That is six units.
Six is where the money coming in has caught the money that went out. The seventh unit is the first one that is profit.
problems.useAgain: when fixed money went out first and every sale claws back the same amount.
hints: Ask how much of the hole one unit fills, then how many of those fit in the hole.
Count up in that size step until you land on the fixed costs.
problems.socraticHint: What happens to the money on the seventh unit that did not happen on the sixth?

variant.prompt: In your head. Suppose fixed costs were 20 dollars and each unit sold leaves 4 dollars. How many units sold gets you back to zero?

problems.prompt: In your head. How many 25 cent coins make 10 dollars?
explanation: Do one dollar first. Four 25 cent coins make a dollar, because 25 four times is 100.
Ten dollars is ten of those piles of four.
Ten fours are 40 coins.
problems.useAgain: when a big amount breaks into equal pieces and you want how many pieces.
hints: Start with one dollar rather than with ten.
Once you know what one dollar takes, do that ten times.
problems.socraticHint: Which is easier to count first, the coins in one dollar or the coins in ten dollars, and why?

variant.prompt: In your head. How many 20 cent coins make 6 dollars?

problem.prompt: On graph paper mark the point 2 across and 3 up. Now fold the paper along the up and down line that sits at 5 across, so the left half lands on the right half. Where does your point land?
explanation: A fold is a mirror. Nothing moves along the fold line, only across it.
The point sits 3 squares to the left of the line at 5 across.
So it lands 3 squares to the right of that line, at 8 across, and its height never changes.
The trap is 7 across, which counts the fold line itself as one of the steps.
problem.useAgain: when a point or a shape is mirrored and you need where it lands without cutting anything out.
hints: Count the squares between your point and the fold line, going sideways only.
It lands the same number of squares on the other side, at the same height.
problem.socraticHint: Which of the two numbers in your point can a sideways fold not touch at all?

variant.prompt: Mark the point 3 across and 4 up, then fold along the up and down line at 6 across. Where does it land?

steps.title: From the story to the equation, and the profit line

problems.prompt:
Jamal solved a run's cost like this: fixed costs were 15 dollars plus 2 dollars of materials for every unit made, and the whole run came to 33 dollars.
Line 1: Write the total as an equation: 15 + 2n = 33.
Line 2: Subtract 15 from both sides: 2n = 18.
Line 3: Divide both sides by 2: n = 9.
Line 4: Check it back: 15 plus 2 times 9 is 35.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 4 is wrong: 15 plus 2 times 9 is 33, not 35.
Lines 1 to 3 are correct: the equation is 15 + 2n = 33, and subtracting 15 gives 2n = 18.
Dividing by 2 gives n = 9.
A real check lands back on the story's total, 33, and line 4's own arithmetic does not.
The equation and the solving were right; the mistake is only in the last line's addition.
problems.useAgain: when you check a cost equation solved for a count of units, since the check line has to land back on the total the story gave.
hints: The equation and the solving steps shown here are correct; the trap is a plain arithmetic slip in the check.
Work out 15 plus 2 times 9 yourself, and compare it with what the worked solution claims.
problems.socraticHint: If a check line is supposed to land back on the number the story started with, does this one?

variant.prompt:
Jamal solved another run: fixed costs were 10 dollars plus 3 dollars of materials for every unit made, and the whole run came to 40 dollars.
Line 1: Write the total as an equation: 10 + 3n = 40.
Line 2: Subtract 10 from both sides: 3n = 30.
Line 3: Divide both sides by 3: n = 9.
Line 4: Check it back: 10 plus 3 times 9 is 37.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Suppose one market charges 8 dollars for the table plus 1 dollar for every unit you sell. Another charges 2 dollars for the table plus 3 dollars for every unit. At how many units sold do the two cost exactly the same?
explanation: Let n be the units sold. One table costs 8 plus n, the other costs 2 plus 3n.
The same cost means one equation: 8 plus n equals 2 plus 3n.
Take n off both pans, then 2 off both, and 6 equals 2n, so n is 3.
Check it: 8 plus 3 is 11, and 2 plus 9 is 11.
problems.useAgain: when the unknown count sits in both pans because both sides charge something per unit.
hints: Write what each market costs for n units before you compare anything.
The letter is in both pans. Take the smaller pile of letters off both sides first.
problems.socraticHint: Below that count, which market is the cheaper one, and does it stay cheaper forever?

variant.prompt: Suppose one market charges 10 dollars for the table plus 2 dollars a unit, and another charges 4 dollars for the table plus 5 dollars a unit. At how many units are they the same?

problems.prompt: Suppose you sold 3 more units on Saturday than on Sunday, and 27 units over the two days. Let n be Sunday's number. Which equation says exactly that?
explanation: n is Sunday, so Saturday is n plus 3.
The two days added together make 27, so n plus n plus 3 equals 27.
That solves to n equals 12, with 15 on Saturday, and 12 and 15 do add to 27.
The trap is n plus 3 equals 27, which describes Saturday on its own and loses Sunday out of the total.
problems.useAgain: when a story compares one day with another and you must choose which day the letter stands for.
hints: Write down in words what n stands for, then write the other day in terms of n.
Over the two days is an addition, and it is what the equals sign is about.
problems.socraticHint: If n had been Saturday instead of Sunday, would any of these four equations still be the true one?

variant.prompt: Suppose you sold 5 fewer units on Sunday than on Saturday, and 33 units over the two days. Let n be Saturday's number. Which equation says exactly that?

problems.prompt: Suppose each unit sells for 4 dollars, its materials cost 1.50 dollars, and the fixed costs of the run were 12 dollars. What is the smallest whole number of units sold that leaves a profit above zero?
explanation: Each unit brings in 4 and costs 1.50, so it leaves 2.50 towards the fixed costs.
Profit is 2.50 times n take away 12, and you want that above zero.
Four units leave 10, which is 2 short. Five units leave 12.50, which is 50 cents clear.
So 5. Four is still a loss, and 4.8 of a unit is not a thing anyone can sell.
problems.useAgain: when a question asks for the first count where money made passes zero rather than reaches it.
hints: Work out what one unit leaves once its own materials are paid.
Fill the 12 dollar hole with that amount, and watch for the first whole unit past it.
problems.socraticHint: At the count where profit is neither above nor below zero, where exactly has the money gone?

variant.prompt: Suppose each unit sells for 5 dollars, its materials cost 2 dollars, and the fixed costs were 15 dollars. What is the smallest whole number of units sold that leaves a profit above zero?

problems.prompt: Keep those numbers: 4 dollars a unit, 1.50 in materials, 12 dollars of fixed costs. Plot units sold across the bottom and profit up the side, with zero profit on the line through the middle. What profit does the point above 4 units sit at, in dollars? A point below the middle line is a negative number.
explanation: Four units bring in 16 dollars and their materials cost 6, so 10 dollars is left.
The fixed 12 dollars still has to come out of that 10.
10 take away 12 is -2, so the point sits 2 dollars under the middle line.
A point under the line is not a mistake. It is the part of the climb before break-even.
problems.useAgain: when a plotted point lands below zero and you have to say what its height means.
hints: Work out the money in and the money out for exactly 4 units before you look at the plot.
Profit below zero is drawn below the middle line, as far below as the number is below zero.
problems.socraticHint: Where on this plot does the point for zero units sit, before anything at all has been sold?

variant.prompt: Same numbers. What profit does the point above 10 units sit at, in dollars?

problems.prompt: Those points lie on one straight line. Going from the point above 4 units to the point above 8 units, how many dollars does the line climb for each extra unit sold?
explanation: The point above 4 units sits at 2 below zero. The point above 8 units sits at 8.
From 2 below zero up to 8 is a climb of 10 dollars, spread over 4 extra units.
10 shared by 4 is 2.50 for each extra unit.
That is the price take away the materials, which is why the climb is the same between any two points on this line.
problems.useAgain: when a line climbs steadily and you want what one step across is worth.
hints: Read the two heights off first, then ask how far apart the two points are across the bottom.
Share the climb between the units you crossed to get it.
problems.socraticHint: If every unit adds the same climb, what has that climb got to do with the number on the price tag?

variant.prompt: Suppose instead the price were 5 dollars and the materials 2 dollars a unit. How many dollars does that line climb for each extra unit sold?

steps.title: The diagonal that finishes the shape, and the streak that almost always breaks

problems.prompt: A TV screen is 24 inches wide and 18 inches tall. What is its diagonal size, in inches?
explanation: A screen's diagonal is the longest side of a right triangle formed by its width and height.
24 squared plus 18 squared is 576 plus 324, which is 900.
The square root of 900 is 30 inches.
problems.useAgain: when a screen or panel's diagonal size is advertised, and its width and height give the two legs.
hints: Square the width and the height, then add them together.
Take the square root of that total for the diagonal.
problems.socraticHint: When a TV's size is given as one number, which measurement of the rectangle is that number actually describing?

variant.prompt: A TV screen is 20 inches wide and 15 inches tall. What is its diagonal size, in inches?

problems.prompt: A rectangular field is 21 m long and 28 m wide. What is the diagonal distance straight across it, in m?
explanation: The diagonal cuts the field into two right triangles, with the length and width as the legs.
21 squared plus 28 squared is 441 plus 784, which is 1225.
The square root of 1225 is 35 m.
problems.useAgain: when the shortest path across a rectangle is needed, cutting straight through instead of along two edges.
hints: The diagonal is shorter than walking the two edges. Which two numbers are the triangle's legs here?
Square both legs, add them, then take the square root.
problems.socraticHint: Is walking straight across the diagonal ever longer than walking along the two edges?

variant.prompt: A rectangular field is 30 m long and 40 m wide. What is the diagonal distance straight across it, in m?

problems.prompt: You flip a fair coin 3 times. What is the probability, as a fraction, of getting at least one head?
explanation: Count the opposite: no heads at all, meaning every flip is tails.
That happens with probability 1/2 times 1/2 times 1/2, which is 1/8.
At least one head is 1 minus 1/8, which is 7/8.
problems.useAgain: when at least one head or success is asked for across several coin flips or similar independent tries.
hints: What is the only way to get zero heads in three flips?
Subtract the all-tails probability from 1.
problems.socraticHint: Out of every possible run of three flips, how many of them have exactly zero heads?

variant.prompt: You flip a fair coin 4 times. What is the probability, as a fraction, of getting at least one head?

problems.prompt: A box has 4 red marbles and 1 blue marble, 5 total. You draw one, replace it, and repeat three times. What is the probability, as a fraction, of drawing at least one blue in the three draws?
explanation: Count the opposite: blue never shows up in any of the three draws.
Each draw avoids blue with probability 4/5, so all three avoiding it is 4/5 times 4/5 times 4/5, which is 64/125.
At least one blue is 1 minus 64/125, which is 61/125.
problems.useAgain: when at least one of a rare outcome is asked for across three or more replaced draws.
hints: Find the probability blue is missing from all three draws first.
Subtract that no-blue-at-all probability from 1.
problems.socraticHint: With three independent draws instead of two, does the chance of missing blue every single time get bigger or smaller?

variant.prompt: A box has 3 red marbles and 2 blue marbles, 5 total. You draw one, replace it, and repeat twice. What is the probability, as a fraction, of drawing at least one blue in the two draws?

steps.title: The traverse: how to sit it
steps.body:
A traverse is not a summit. It is the long crossing from peak to peak along a ridge, where the work is not one hard move but staying steady over eight of them without coming off.

Eight peaks, mixed on purpose. Numbers, shapes, money, coins, angles, a walk to the shop. Nothing tells you which idea a peak wants, and working that out is most of the climb. That is exactly what a mixed set does that a page of the same kind never can.

Four rules, and they are the whole method.

One sitting. Start them together and finish them together, in one go, so the ridge is crossed rather than sampled.

No clock. There is no timer on this. Not a sand timer, not a phone, nothing. Take the time each peak takes. The only timer in this house belongs to debate, and it stays there.

Field journal open. Every peak gets working on the page, not just an answer: what you noticed, what you tried, and the drawing if there was one. An answer with no working is a peak you cannot show anybody.

Order is yours. Read all eight first, start with the one that looks friendliest, and leave anything that stalls you. Put a small circle beside a peak you left and come back along the ridge for it at the end. A peak circled and returned to is climbing. A peak stared at for twenty minutes is standing still.

When the eight are done, mark each one honestly: got it, got it but was unsure, or did not get it. That third mark is the useful one, and it is the reason nothing here is timed.

problems.prompt: Invent your own counting problem that needs casework to solve, in the shape of the coin, digit or triangle problems from this season. State the question, split it into cases the way this season always did, say why your cases cover everything and never overlap, then give the final count.

mustMention: cases that cover every possibility with nothing missed
the final count, computed from the cases

explanation: Choose a counting question where splitting into cases is the natural move.
This season split by tens digit, by coin count or by longest side.
Say what you are splitting on before you list a single case.
Argue that your cases cover everything and that no possibility could ever land in two of them at once.
Add the cases together for your final count, and check a small piece of it by hand.
problems.useAgain: when you want to build your own counting question and prove your list of cases is really complete.
hints: Decide what you are splitting on before you invent the rest of the question around it.
A case that can hide, or a case that overlaps another, breaks the proof even if your final number happens to be right.
problems.socraticHint: Could a stranger check whether your cases overlap without you telling them the final count first?

problems.prompt: The three angles of a triangle are in the ratio 1 to 2 to 3. How many degrees is the biggest angle?
explanation: Call the smallest angle one share. Then the others are two shares and three shares.
That is six equal shares altogether, and the angles of any triangle add to 180 degrees.
180 shared into 6 is 30, so one share is 30 degrees.
The biggest angle is three shares, which is 90. The triangle turns out to be right angled.
problems.useAgain: when a whole is cut in a given ratio and you can call the smallest part one share.
hints: Add the numbers in the ratio to see how many equal shares the triangle is cut into.
Find what one share is worth in degrees before you touch the biggest angle.
problems.socraticHint: Which single angle, once you knew it, would hand you the other two for free?

variant.prompt: The three angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 to 3 to 4. How many degrees is the biggest angle?

problems.prompt: A square 10 cm on each side has a square 4 cm on each side cut out of one of its corners. What is the perimeter of the shape that is left, in cm?
explanation: Draw it. The cut takes 4 cm off the end of the top edge and 4 cm off the end of the right edge.
But it also adds two new 4 cm edges where the corner used to be, going in and then back out.
What came off and what went on are the same 8 cm, so the perimeter stays at 40.
The area did fall, by 16 square cm. Area and perimeter do not have to move together.
problems.useAgain: when a piece is cut out of a shape and you have to say what the boundary did.
hints: Draw it and walk your pencil all the way round, saying each edge length out loud.
Some edges got shorter and two new ones appeared. Compare what was lost with what was added.
problems.socraticHint: Would your answer change if the cut-out square were 2 cm instead of 4 cm, and what does that tell you?

variant.prompt: A square 12 cm on each side has a square 5 cm on each side cut out of one corner. What is the perimeter of the shape that is left, in cm?

problems.prompt: A tag reads 50 dollars. In the morning the price goes up 20 percent. In the afternoon the new price comes down 20 percent. What does the tag read at the end of the day, in dollars?
explanation: 20 percent of 50 is 10, so the morning price is 60 dollars.
The afternoon cut is 20 percent of 60, not of 50, because the tag now says 60. That is 12.
60 take away 12 is 48 dollars.
The two percents are the same size but they are shares of different numbers, so they never cancel out.
problems.useAgain: when one percent change follows another and you have to ask what each one is a share of.
hints: Work out the morning price and write it down before you touch the afternoon.
Ask which number the afternoon percent is a share of.
problems.socraticHint: If the day had run the other way round, down first and then up, would the tag land anywhere different?

variant.prompt: A tag reads 80 dollars, goes up 25 percent in the morning, and then the new price comes down 25 percent. What does the tag read at the end of the day, in dollars?

problems.prompt: You walk to the shop at 3 km an hour and walk home along the same road at 6 km an hour. What is your average speed for the whole trip, in km an hour?
explanation: Put a real distance on the road, one that suits both speeds. Say the shop is 6 km away.
Out takes 2 hours at 3 km an hour. Home takes 1 hour at 6 km an hour.
That is 12 km walked in 3 hours, which is 4 km an hour.
The trap is 4.5, halfway between the speeds. You spend longer at the slow speed, so it pulls harder.
problems.useAgain: when two rates cover the same distance and you need the rate for the whole journey.
hints: Averaging the two numbers is the trap. Put a real distance on the road first.
Work out the time each leg takes, then share the whole distance by the whole time.
problems.socraticHint: Which leg of the walk takes up more of your afternoon, and should it count for more or for less?

variant.prompt: You walk out at 2 km an hour and walk back along the same road at 3 km an hour. What is your average speed for the whole trip, in km an hour?

problems.prompt: You pay exactly 25 cents using only 5 cent and 10 cent coins, as many of each as you like. How many different ways are there?
explanation: Try them all, but in order, counting by how many 10 cent coins you use.
Two tens leaves 5 cents, so one five. One ten leaves 15, so three fives. No tens leaves 25, so five fives.
Three tens would already be 30, too much, so the list stops there.
Three ways. Walking the list in order is what makes it complete instead of hopeful.
That is try them all: when only a few sizes are possible, test every one in order instead of hoping you found them all.
problems.useAgain: when only a few sizes are possible and the whole list can be walked in order.
hints: Count by the bigger coin, starting with as many of them as will fit.
For each number of tens, ask whether the rest can be made of fives at all.
problems.socraticHint: What would go wrong if you counted by the 5 cent coins instead, and would the answer come out the same?

variant.prompt: You pay exactly 30 cents using only 5 cent and 10 cent coins. How many different ways are there?

problems.prompt: Two pencils and one eraser cost 1.30 dollars. One pencil and one eraser cost 0.85 dollars. What does one pencil cost, in dollars?
explanation: Put the two baskets side by side. The second one has a pencil fewer and nothing else different.
So the whole gap between 1.30 and 0.85 is that one missing pencil.
1.30 take away 0.85 is 0.45, so a pencil costs 0.45.
The eraser never had to be found, though it comes out at 0.40 if you want it.
problems.useAgain: when two totals differ by exactly one item and you want that item's price.
hints: Line the two baskets up and cross off everything they have in common.
Whatever is left on one side has to explain the whole difference in money.
problems.socraticHint: What is in the first basket that is not in the second, and what is in the second that is not in the first?

variant.prompt: Three cups and one plate cost 2.40 dollars. Two cups and one plate cost 1.80 dollars. What does one cup cost, in dollars?

problems.prompt: Multiply 2027 threes together. What is the last digit of the answer?
explanation: Only the last digit matters, so watch it: 3, 9, 27, 81, 243.
The last digits run 3, 9, 7, 1 and then start over, because each step only multiplies the last digit by 3.
So the pattern loops every four threes, and 2027 is 4 times 506 with 3 left over.
Three left over lands on the third one in the loop, which is 7.
problems.useAgain: when a power gets enormous and only the last digit or a remainder is being asked for.
hints: Write out the first five or six powers of 3 and look only at their last digits.
Find where the last digits start repeating, and count how long that loop is.
problems.socraticHint: Where in the loop does the very first three sit, and does the counting start at zero or at one?

variant.prompt: Multiply 2027 sevens together. What is the last digit of the answer?

steps.title: The month 3 monster: the bridge and the flashlight

problems.prompt: The month 3 monster gets its ending today, cracked or retired with honours. Four hikers reach a rope bridge in the dark. There is one flashlight, the bridge holds two at a time, and nobody crosses without the flashlight, so somebody has to walk it back. On their own the four take 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes, and a pair crosses at the slower one's pace. Almost everybody who meets this puzzle lands on 19 minutes. Beat 19, and then argue that your answer cannot be beaten.

mustMention: all four are across in 17 minutes
there are always three crossings out and two walks back
sending the 5 and the 10 apart costs at least 19

explanation: The 19 everyone finds walks the 1 back with the flashlight every single time.
Cross the 5 and the 10 together instead, and the 5 costs nothing of its own.
1 and 2 out, 1 back, 5 and 10 out, 2 back, 1 and 2 out. Seventeen minutes.
Now the floor. Four hikers always need three crossings out and two walks back.
Sent apart, 5 and 10 cost 10 and 5, the third crossing at least 2, each walk back at least 1: 19.
Sent together they cost 10, and the other two crossings out cost at least 2 each. The walks back cannot both be the 1, who would then be on all three crossings, so 17.
problems.useAgain: when a best answer has been found and the harder half is proving nothing can beat it.
hints: Nineteen comes from one habit: the fastest hiker carries the flashlight back every time. Break that habit and see what it buys.
The 10 has to cross at some point, and that crossing costs 10 whoever is beside it. Ask what else could be getting across during those same 10 minutes.
problems.socraticHint: How many times does the flashlight have to come back at all, and does that number depend on who is carrying it?

variant.prompt: The same bridge and the same rules, but the four hikers take 1, 2, 6 and 8 minutes. What is the fastest everyone can be across, and how do you know nothing beats it?

mustMention: all four are across in 15 minutes
the 1 and the 2 do all of the walking back

steps.title: Explain it in writing
steps.prompt: Two plots on one sheet of graph paper. First, units sold across the bottom against profit up the side, at one price, with four points on it. Second, your week 6 table: price across the bottom against the profit that table predicted, one point for each price you tried. Then write which plot makes a straight line and which one bends, and why. Say what one step across is worth on the straight one, in dollars, and say why the bending one has no such number at all.

steps.title: Explain back
steps.prompt: Record yourself teaching the walk to the shop and back: why the answer is not the number halfway between 3 and 6, using a distance you picked yourself and the two times it gives. Then name the peak from the traverse you would hand a friend first, and say what made you pick that one.
